en: PAGASA monitors the Philippine Area of Responsibility, a specific zone where tropical cyclones are tracked and given local names.
The Amihan, or northeast monsoon, brings cool and dry weather to the Philippines between November and February.
Volcanic ash from Mount Pinatubo's 1991 eruption enriched the soil in Central Luzon, significantly boosting subsequent agricultural harvests.
Philippine adobe, a porous volcanic rock, was historically used by early settlers to build the stone walls of Intramuros.
The Puerto Princesa Subterranean River in Palawan features an underground river that flows directly out into the sea.
Filipino farmers traditionally use the Balatik constellation, a local star pattern in Orion, to signal the planting season.
During a full moon, the highest tides in Manila Bay occur due to the aligned gravitational pull of the sun and moon.
The Manila Trench is a deep oceanic canyon formed by the subduction of the Philippine Sea Plate under the Eurasian Plate.
Mayon Volcano in Albay is famous for its perfect conical shape, which is built up by layers of hardened lava and ash.
The Sierra Madre mountains block Pacific moisture, creating a drier rain shadow climate across the Central Luzon plains.
During an El Niño event, the Philippines experiences severe droughts that dry up local dams and reduce hydroelectric power.
The Chocolate Hills in Bohol consist of thousands of cone-shaped limestone mounds formed from ancient marine coral fossils.
